To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the performance of a class of weighted additive-increase-multiple-decrease (AIM) algorithms for scalable service differentiation is limited by the fact that they do not scale well in terms of fairness and throughput.

(1) loss adaptation is critical to scalable differentiated service, (2) estimating loss characteristics using only end-to-end mechanisms, such as packet losses, is inherently difficult, and (3) the loss adaptive weighted AIM algorithm is a scalable service differentiation mechanism.

(1) the loss characteristics of a connection are critical in determining the performance of service differentiation algorithms, and (2) the estimation of loss characteristics is an inherently difficult and error-prone problem, and therefore the use of purely end-to-end loss estimation mechanisms for service differentiation is limited in practice.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of scalable service differentiation mechanisms for TCP/IP networks.
the following question: Can service differentiation be achieved using purely end-to- end mechanisms?
the design and analysis of scalable end-to-end service differentiation mechanisms that are robust to loss characteristics and network dynamics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
scalable service differentiation using purely network layer mechanisms is a challenging problem.
the end-to-end mechanisms alone cannot achieve scalable service differentiation.
service differentiation via weighted congestion control mechanisms is possible, but is not easy to achieve.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the AIMD principle is a very powerful principle for congestion control, but it is not sufficient by itself for service differentiation.
the use of end-to-end mechanisms for service differentiation is feasible but challenging.
the use of end-to-end congestion controls is an effective approach to service differentiation, but it has limitations in scalability.
The main takeaway from our work is that
scalable service differentiation using purely congestion control mechanisms is not a trivial exercise.
the AIMD principle, when applied to a large number of flows, does not scale well to achieve high performance service differentiation.
scalable end-to-end service differentiation is a challenging problem.
